## Two coordinates, one name

Ask how far it is from C to E and there are two honest answers. Count letter
names inclusively, C then D then E, and you have a third. Count equal-tempered
semitones and you have four. Letters give you the size. Semitones give you the
quality. Hold both at once and the pair finally has a name: major third.

Sound reports only one of those coordinates. C-sharp to E and D-flat to E each
span three semitones, and your speakers render them identically. On paper they
part company, because C to E covers three letters and D to E covers two, so one
is a third and the other a second. No amount of careful listening recovers the
spelling; the spelling was never in the air. That's the practical reason Lesson
10 kept a letter beside every MIDI number, and it's why the helper below takes
hashes and not bare integers.

That helper handles a narrow domain on purpose: simple ascending pairs whose
expected quality comes out major or perfect. Read it as a first join between
letter space and semitone space.

## Name a pair, then hear it

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 72

letters = {c: 0, d: 1, e: 2, f: 3, g: 4, a: 5, b: 6}
base_distance = {1 => 0, 2 => 2, 3 => 4, 4 => 5, 5 => 7, 6 => 9, 7 => 11, 8 => 12}

define :interval_name do |first, second, letter_map, distances|
  size = ((letter_map[second[:letter]] - letter_map[first[:letter]]) % 7) + 1
  semitones = second[:pitch] - first[:pitch]
  expected = distances[size]
  quality = semitones == expected ? ([1,4,5,8].include?(size) ? "perfect" : "major") : "altered"
  "#{quality} #{size}"
end

c = {letter: :c, pitch: note(:c4)}
e = {letter: :e, pitch: note(:e4)}
puts interval_name(c, e, letters, base_distance)
play c[:pitch]; sleep 1; play e[:pitch]
```

You get `major 3` in the log, then C, then E. Those two `play` calls supply the
four semitones. The hashes supply the letters that turn four semitones into a
third. Now edit `letter: :e` to `letter: :f` and leave `pitch:` exactly as it
is. Which output changes, the printed name or the sound?

## Break one coordinate at a time

1. Add the pairs C–F and C–F-sharp. Both cover the letters C, D, E, F, so both
   stay fourths. That extra semitone in F-sharp turns perfect into augmented,
   and the helper as written reports it as `altered`.
2. Restore the original, then run C-sharp–E against D-flat–E. Print the MIDI
   difference and the letter size for each. You'll see the distances agree while
   the sizes disagree.
3. Restore C–E and swap the two hashes so the pair descends. Before you touch
   the arithmetic, decide whether the result should carry direction as its own
   field or normalise everything into an ascending interval. That's an interface
   decision, so make it in words first.

## Where size and quality come from

Interval naming is a join across two coordinate systems. The `letters` hash maps
seven names onto a cycle. Subtract the indices modulo seven, add one, and you
get an inclusive ordinal size: same letter is a unison, adjacent letters make a
second, and so on round the cycle. MIDI subtraction answers the other question
without consulting a single letter.

`base_distance` records how many semitones an unaltered interval of each size
contains. Sizes 1, 4, 5 and 8 belong to the perfect family; sizes 2, 3, 6 and 7
belong to the major and minor family. Comparing the actual count against that
baseline gives you the quality. For a third, four semitones is major, three is
minor, five is augmented, two is diminished. For a fourth, five is perfect, six
is augmented, four is diminished. Letters choose which vocabulary applies; the
semitone count then picks a word out of it.

Drop either coordinate and the naming collapses in a specific way. With MIDI
alone the helper counts four semitones and has to invent a spelling before it
can say "third." With letters alone it counts a third and can't tell you whether
that third is major, minor, diminished or augmented.

Two extensions are waiting. Compound intervals continue the inclusive count past
the octave, and descending pairs need a direction policy. Add them one at a
time, or a single wrong label will have several plausible causes.

Lesson 19 stops calculating and starts listening. The names come from this
two-coordinate system; recognising them by ear is a separate skill that grows
from repeated hearings.

## Fill in the missing qualities

Extend `interval_name` so it returns diminished, minor, major, perfect and
augmented for simple ascending intervals inside an octave. Build explicitly
spelled test pairs from C to every chromatic pitch you need, and include the
enharmonic alternatives wherever one semitone count can carry two different
sizes.

Assert an expected label for every case and print the semitone distance beside
it. Run those assertions as a data check first, then audition a few of the pairs
in Sonic Pi 5. A correct label proves the rules joined spelling to distance.
Hearing the same interval and naming it without the log is the next lesson's
work.
